modelAnswer: The primary lipid of myelin is galactocerebroside (also called cerebroside). Sphingolipids such as galactocerebroside and sulfatide constitute the predominant lipids of the myelin sheath, accounting for about 25-30% of myelin dry weight. Their hydrophobic character is critical for the insulating properties of myelin, allowing saltatory conduction of nerve impulses.

Touch receptors (e.g., Pacinian corpuscles, Meissner corpuscles) are rapidly adapting receptors that respond to changes in stimulus intensity but stop firing during sustained stimulation, allowing the CNS to detect new stimuli. Pain receptors (nociceptors, e.g., free nerve endings) are slowly adapting receptors that continue firing as long as the damaging stimulus is present, ensuring the body is continuously warned of tissue injury.

Properties of receptors include: 1) Specificity (receptors are sensitive to a specific form of energy called the adequate stimulus). 2) Transduction (conversion of stimulus energy into generator/receptor potentials). 3) Adaptation (reduction in firing rate during constant stimulation, classified as rapidly or slowly adapting). 4) Threshold (minimum stimulus intensity needed to evoke a response). 5) Sensory coding (intensity, duration, localization, and modality are encoded by frequency, receptor type, and fiber projection).

Receptor adaptation occurs when a sustained stimulus produces a progressive decrease in generator potential amplitude despite constant stimulus intensity. Mechanisms include: 1) Inactivation or closure of ion channels responsible for the receptor potential. 2) Opening of potassium channels that hyperpolarize the receptor membrane. 3) Structural changes in the receptor capsule that reduce mechanical transduction (e.g., Pacinian corpuscle lamellae filter sustained pressure). 4) Inactivation of voltage-gated calcium channels at the sensory nerve terminal.

Paradoxical cold sensation occurs when a warm stimulus applied to a cold spot (an area of skin rich in cold receptors) is perceived as cold. This happens because certain cold receptors can be stimulated not only by cold but also by very warm temperatures. The incorrect temperature perception arises from the specific pattern of nerve fiber activation rather than from true thermoreceptor specificity.

Crude touch sensation is carried by the anterior spinothalamic tract, uses mechanical receptors (tactile discs, Ruffini endings), and transmitted by A-beta and A-delta fibers. Thermal sensation (heat/cold) is carried by the lateral spinothalamic tract, uses thermoreceptors (free nerve endings), and transmitted by A-delta and C fibers. Crude touch receptors have larger receptive fields and lower spatial resolution compared to thermal receptors.

Pain receptors (nociceptors) are stimulated by: 1) Mechanical injury (deformation, pressure, stretching). 2) Thermal injury (extreme heat >45°C or extreme cold). 3) Chemical mediators released from damaged tissue (bradykinin, histamine, prostaglandins, substance P, hydrogen ions, potassium ions). 4) Ischemia leading to accumulation of acidic metabolites. Some nociceptors are polymodal and respond to multiple stimuli.

Reflex movements require: sensory receptor stimulation, afferent nerve transmission, central synapse in the spinal cord or brainstem, efferent nerve transmission, and effector muscle contraction. They are involuntary, stereotyped, rapid, and do not require cortical involvement. Voluntary movements require: conscious intention, cortical planning (prefrontal/premotor cortex), corticospinal tract execution, and feedback from proprioceptors. They are learned, variable, and require higher cortical centers.

Clinical importance of stretch reflex: 1) Maintains muscle tone and posture by continuously adjusting muscle length. 2) Monosynaptic knee-jerk (patellar tendon reflex) and ankle-jerk (Achilles reflex) are standard clinical tests for spinal cord and peripheral nerve integrity. 3) Absence indicates lower motor neuron lesion or peripheral neuropathy. 4) Hyperreflexia indicates upper motor neuron lesion. 5) Tests segmental integrity of spinal cord segments L2-L4 and S1-S2.

Nuclear bag fibers are larger, have more nuclei clustered in an expanded central bag region, are more elastic, and respond primarily to dynamic stretch (rate of change in length). Nuclear chain fibers are smaller, have nuclei arranged in a linear chain, are less elastic, and respond mainly to static stretch (sustained length). Nuclear bag fibers signal muscle velocity, while nuclear chain fibers signal muscle position.

Sleep stages and EEG patterns:
1) Stage N1 (light sleep): theta waves (4-7 Hz), low amplitude.
2) Stage N2: sleep spindles (12-14 Hz bursts) and K-complexes.
3) Stage N3 (slow-wave/deep sleep): delta waves (0.5-4 Hz), high amplitude.
4) REM sleep: low-amplitude, mixed-frequency waves resembling wakefulness (desynchronized EEG), with rapid eye movements and muscle atonia.

Urea is synthesized in the hepatocytes of the liver via the urea cycle, which converts toxic ammonia (from amino acid deamination) into urea. The urea cycle consumes ammonia, bicarbonate, and aspartate to produce urea, fumarate, and water. The synthesized urea is then transported via the bloodstream to the kidneys, where it is filtered by the glomeruli and excreted in urine, representing the primary route for nitrogen disposal from protein metabolism.

The urea cycle and citric acid cycle are metabolically linked through aspartate and fumarate. The urea cycle consumes aspartate (donating its amino group to form argininosuccinate). Fumarate, a byproduct of argininosuccinate cleavage, enters the citric acid cycle and can be converted to malate and then oxaloacetate. Oxaloacetate can be transaminated back to aspartate, completing the cycle. Additionally, carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I uses bicarbonate derived from TCA cycle intermediates.

Ipsilateral loss of proprioception and vibration below level of lesion
Contralateral loss of proprioception and vibration below level of lesion
explanation: Brown-Sequard syndrome (hemisection of spinal cord) produces: ipsilateral UMN paralysis and loss of proprioception/vibration/fine touch below the lesion; contralateral loss of pain and temperature below the lesion. Contralateral loss of proprioception does NOT occur.

modelAnswer: The major genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease is the apolipoprotein E (APOE) epsilon-4 allele. APOE4 carriers have a significantly increased risk of developing both early-onset and late-onset AD. APOE4 impairs amyloid-beta clearance, promotes aggregation, and affects lipid metabolism in neurons. Having one copy increases risk ~3-fold; two copies increase risk ~12-15-fold. Other genes include APP, PSEN1, PSEN2 (autosomal dominant early-onset forms).

Clinical features distinguishing frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) from Alzheimer's disease include: 1) FTLD presents with early behavioral changes (disinhibition, apathy, compulsions) or language deficits, while memory and spatial orientation are relatively preserved early on. 2) AD presents with early anterograde amnesia and progressive memory loss. 3) FTLD onset is typically earlier (45-65 years) compared to AD. 4) FTLD shows frontal and temporal lobe atrophy on imaging, while AD shows hippocampal and medial temporal lobe atrophy.

Autosomal dominant Parkinson's disease is caused by mutations in: 1) SNCA (alpha-synuclein) gene on chromosome 4 - the first identified PD gene, leading to Lewy body formation. 2) LRRK2 (leucine-rich repeat kinase 2) on chromosome 12 - the most common cause of familial PD, especially in certain ethnic groups (Ashkenazi Jewish and North African Berber). 3) VPS35 (vacuolar protein sorting 35). Rarer genes include PARK7, PINK1, and PRKN, which typically cause recessive juvenile-onset PD rather than autosomal dominant forms.

Frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) most commonly shows autosomal dominant inheritance. The most frequent genetic cause is mutations in the MAPT (microtubule-associated protein tau) gene on chromosome 17, which encodes the tau protein. Other autosomal dominant causes include mutations in GRN (progranulin) and C9orf72 (hexanucleotide repeat expansion). Approximately 30-40% of FTLD cases have a family history, and genetic testing often reveals pathogenic variants in these three genes.
